extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged public and readers of political pamphlets (late-18th-century British/international audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A political pamphlet rebutting Edmund Burke's criticisms of the French Revolution and setting out principles about law, legitimacy, and revolution. It argues how governments and laws should be judged and when popular revolt is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posterity cannot be bound forever by past human power
rubrics_metrics.description: From what, or from whence, does Mr. Burke prove the right of any human power to bind posterity for ever? ... If it ever existed it must now exist, for whatever appertains to the nature of man cannot be annihilated by man. ... He must, therefore, prove that his Adam possessed such a power, or such a right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clauses attempting to make authority 'immortal' are inherently null and void because immortal power is not a human right. A Parliament cannot validly found a perpetual dominion over future generations; attempts to do so are 'a formality of words' without legitimate force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws derive their force from the consent of the living
rubrics_metrics.description: Although laws made in one generation often continue in force through succeeding generations, yet they continue to derive their force from the consent of the living. A law not repealed continues in force, not because it cannot be repealed, but because it is not repealed; and the non-repealing passes for consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the ongoing legitimacy of laws by whether living people consent (actively or by non-repeal), not by any putative eternal authority claimed by past legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government is for the living, not the dead
rubrics_metrics.description: The circumstances of the world are continually changing, and the opinions of men change also; and as government is for the living, and not for the dead, it is the living only that has any right in it. That which may be thought right ... in one age may be thought wrong ... in another. In such cases, who is to decide, the living or the dead?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about governance and lawfulness should be made by those alive to experience their consequences; political institutions should not be treated as immutable heirs of remote authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish revolt against principles from revolt against persons
rubrics_metrics.description: It was not against Louis XVI. but against the despotic principles of the Government, that the nation revolted. ... The Monarch and the Monarchy were distinct and separate things; and it was against the established despotism of the latter, and not against the person or principles of the former, that the revolt commenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging revolutions, assess whether the action targets entrenched oppressive systems and principles rather than merely attacking individual office-holders; such distinction makes revolutions more defensible and less vindictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrenched, distributed despotism can justify systemic revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: When despotism has established itself for ages in a country ... it is not in the person of the king only that it resides. It has its standard everywhere. Every office and department has its despotism, founded upon custom and usage. ... Against this species of despotism ... there is no mode of redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If despotism is institutionalized across many offices and customs, piecemeal reform is inadequate; evaluate the necessity of comprehensive revolution where ordinary redress mechanisms are blocked.

rubrics_metrics.name: When crisis requires action, commit fully or do not attempt
rubrics_metrics.description: When it becomes necessary to do anything, the whole heart and soul should go into the measure, or not attempt it. That crisis was then arrived, and there remained no choice but to act with determined vigor, or not to act at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial or half-hearted measures in moments of systemic crisis risk failure; decisive, wholehearted action is presented as the only responsible option when institutions are in imminent peril.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/political writing should prioritize truth over theatrical dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Burke should recollect that he is writing history, and not plays, and that his readers will expect truth, and not the spouting rant of high-toned exclamation. ... his book is a dramatic performance; ... by the poetical liberties he has taken of omitting some facts, distorting others, and making the whole machinery bend to produce a stage effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques and histories must avoid theatrical exaggeration, omission of causes (e.g., plots), and manufactured facts; evaluate such works by their fidelity to cause-and-effect rather than rhetorical flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge popular violence in context of government-instigated causes and plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Burke has spoken a great deal about plots, but he has never once spoken of this plot against the National Assembly ... It suits his purpose to exhibit the consequences without their causes. ... Whom has the National Assembly brought to the scaffold? None. They were themselves the devoted victims of this plot, and they have not retaliated; why, then, are they charged with revenge they have not acted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing acts of popular violence (e.g., taking the Bastille, extrajudicial killings), consider the proximate causes (plots, threats, imminent danger) and who instigated those threats rather than attributing all excesses to revolutionary principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments' public cruelties teach the populace to imitate cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: They learn it from the governments they live under; and retaliate the punishments they have been accustomed to behold. ... The heads stuck upon spikes ... differed nothing in the horror of the scene from those carried about upon spikes at Paris; yet this was done by the English Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate responsibility for barbarous reprisals by tracing cultural precedents in governmental punishments; to prevent cycles of revenge, governments should abolish cruel spectacles and 'teach governments humanity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary excesses often reflect prior social degradation, not the revolution's principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Admitting [the theatrical exaggerations and outrages] to be true, they show the necessity of the French Revolution, as much as any one thing he could have asserted. These outrages were not the effect of the principles of the Revolution, but of the degraded mind that existed before the Revolution, and which the Revolution is calculated to reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the moral character of a revolution, separate pre-existing social degradation (which breeds mob excess) from the professed principles of the revolutionary movement; reforms should be judged by their capacity to instruct and elevate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy rests on living sentiments and present will, not ancient parchments
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of referring to musty records and mouldy parchments to prove that the rights of the living are lost, 'renounced and abdicated for ever,' by those who are now no more, M. de la Fayette applies to the living world, and emphatically says: 'Call to mind the sentiments which nature has engraved on the heart of every citizen ... For a nation to love liberty, it is sufficient that she knows it; and to be free, it is sufficient that she wills it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political legitimacy by current, natural sentiments and the active will of the people rather than appeals to distant documents or historical acts purporting to bind posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique should examine omitted facts (plots, context) as much as presented consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: It is to be observed throughout Mr. Burke's book that he never speaks of plots against the Revolution; and it is from those plots that all the mischiefs have arisen. It suits his purpose to exhibit the consequences without their causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good political analysis must identify and weigh omitted causes (e.g., conspiracy, military maneuvers) and not only catalogue consequences; omission is a key indicator of biased or theatrical argumentation.
